# Paid call spend bounding

**Need.** A loop that calls a paid interface has a third dimension beside time and space, and it is the only one nobody states. Reading the code tells a reviewer how long it runs and how much it holds; nothing in it says what it may spend, so a bug that would merely be slow against a free endpoint instead buys something, on every retry, while the tests pass and the review approves. The failure is never in the loop body. It is that the call site shipped without anybody writing down what it was allowed to cost, and the first time the number is discussed is on the invoice.

**Input.** The call site being written or changed, what it bills through and per what unit at today's price, every path that can enter it more than once including the retries the platform performs on its own, and which bound the author can set themselves as against the one that needs somebody holding billing authority.

**Core action.** Work out what can re-enter the call before choosing any number, state what the call site may spend per run and per day in currency as well as in calls, place that bound both in the code and where a bug in the code cannot reach it, and decide what happens at the limit according to whether anybody is waiting on the answer.

**Output.** A call site whose two bounds fail independently, a stated behaviour at the limit that matches whether the path is background or user facing, and a record of what could re-enter the call, what price the numbers were chosen against, and who holds the bound the author could not set.

## Activities

1. List every path that can enter this call more than once, including retries the platform performs for you *(observe; re-entry)*
2. Establish what one call costs today and what an ordinary run of them costs *(observe; price)*
3. Choose the bound per run and per day, in calls and in currency *(decide; bound)*
4. Decide what happens at the limit, according to whether somebody is waiting on the call *(decide; limit-behaviour)*
5. Place the bound in the code and again where code cannot reach it *(act; place)*
6. Record what the numbers assume and who holds the bound the author could not set *(deliver; record)*

## Outcomes

### no-paid-call-ships-unbounded

A call site that spends money does not reach the main branch without a bound stated in currency.

- The bound exists as a number per run and per day, in currency as well as in calls, rather than as an intention to keep an eye on it
- A bound the author cannot set themselves is named together with the person who can, and the call site does not ship before that bound exists
- The record says what one call cost at the time the number was chosen, so a later price change is visible as the thing that invalidated it rather than as a mystery

### the-two-bounds-fail-independently

The bound inside the code and the bound outside it cannot be removed by the same mistake.

- The two bounds do not read the same configuration value or environment variable, because one bad deploy would then lift both at once
- The bound outside the code sits where the person writing the code cannot quietly raise it in the same change that needs raising
- A run that stopped at a bound is distinguishable in the record from a run that finished, because a silent stop reads as success and is acted on as one

### the-limit-behaviour-matches-who-is-waiting

Reaching the limit degrades a user facing path and halts a background one, rather than doing the same thing to both.

- A path with somebody waiting on it serves something at the limit, whether stale, cheaper or queued, rather than failing closed and turning a spend control into an outage
- A background or batch path halts at the limit and says so, rather than continuing quietly on a smaller budget nobody chose
- Which of the two a call site is, is written down beside it, because the answer changes the day the same function is called from a new place

## Guidance

Dollars are the third complexity dimension, and the one nobody states. The bug is never in the loop body; it is that the call site shipped without a number. A bound only in code dies with a bug in that code, and a bound only at the provider takes the product down during ordinary traffic, so place both and do not let them share a value. Local testing is not an exemption. What happens at the limit depends on whether anybody is waiting.

## Where this is worth adopting

- A team adding image or video generation to a product, where the list the loop iterates over arrives from a webhook the platform retries, so a loop that obviously terminates doubles the work it does every time the callback fires again.
- An agent that chooses its own next step from model output, where nothing in the code states a depth at which it stops asking, and the cost of each decision is paid before anybody reads the answer.
- A developer wiring a paid endpoint into a prototype on their own machine and treating local work as exempt, when the key in their environment bills the same account that production bills.
- A search or recommendation path that calls a billed model once per request, where a hard daily cap added for safety would take the feature down in the middle of ordinary traffic and nobody has decided what it ought to serve instead.
- A team that has already had one surprise invoice and responded with alerting, which reports afterwards how much was spent rather than preventing the spend, because an alert is not a bound.

}
